hook: A shark-shaped hole swimming through water is a fun, almost cartoonish idea, and the file is very short. Read it slowly anyway, because the last few lines are where the article really lives. The fluorescent-dye detail in the procedures is worth picturing as you go.
whyItMatters: The closing question on the found note matches the article's are-we-cool-yet tag, which frames the shark as something made to make a point rather than a stray animal. It is a neat example of how a few lines of text can change what an object is about.
thingsToNotice:
The procedures read like an ordinary aquarium manual until the dyes come up: the only way to see the shark's insides is to feed it something it cannot digest, and the glowing dye then traces a gut and blood vessels inside a shape that holds nothing at all.

The acquisition log is blunt: at a public pool the shark killed two swimmers and mauled a lifeguard, and the stampede that followed killed five more. The handwritten page pinned to the staff board turns that count into the thesis, arguing that the idea of a shark is deadlier than a real one, and even deadlier than no shark. Its lack of fingerprints, and the smug question it ends on, imply that someone built the empty shark on purpose as a statement about panic.
